column2: Who on earth treats beasts, birds, wild animals and the poor when they are sick? Mostly they are not afflicted.
Disease attacks even fierce, unassailable kings of terrible energy, and takes them as a butcher takes beasts.
Thus the world, silent, flooded with delusion and sorrow, is suddenly swept by a current and carried by a stronger one.
Not by wealth, nor by kingdom, nor by fierce austerity do embodied beings escape the natures to which they are bound.
They would not die nor grow old, all would have all they desire, and none would see the unpleasant, as the fruit of their effort.
Everyone in the world wishes to be above others and strives as he can, but it does not turn out so.
The intoxicated with the pride of lordship and with the pride of wine are attended by the unwearied, the crafty, the cruel and the bold.
For some, afflictions turn back unforeseen; for others one's own and the other's are again lost; nothing at all is reached.
A great inequality of fruit is seen at the joints of action: some carry the palanquin, others go riding in palanquins.
Among all who desire prosperity, others go ahead of chariots; men with a hundred wives, and women by hundreds as widows.
Among beings delighting in the pairs, men go one by one; see this other, supreme; you will make a mere delusion.
Give up dharma and adharma; give up both truth and untruth; having given up both truth and untruth, give up that by which you give up.
This highest secret has been told to you, best of sages, by which gods, leaving the world of mortals, have gone to heaven.
[Bhishma said:] Hearing Narada's words, Shuka of supreme intelligence, steadfast, pondered in his mind and did not arrive at a decision.
With sons and wives is great affliction, in studying the tradition is great toil; what then would be the eternal state, of little affliction and great content?
Then, thinking for a moment, knowing the high and low of dharma, he found his own settled goal, the supreme path of the highest good.

How may I go to the supreme goal unafflicted, and not return again to the ocean of rebirth in wombs?
mahabharata:12:318.50	I long for the supreme state from which one does not return, giving up all attachments, the settled course of the mind.
mahabharata:12:318.51	I shall go where the self will find peace for me, where I shall stand imperishable, unchanging and eternal.
mahabharata:12:318.52	That supreme goal cannot be reached without yoga; for a freed one, no bondage arises from deeds.
mahabharata:12:318.53	Therefore, taking up yoga and leaving the body of the house, becoming wind, I shall enter the sun, the mass of splendour.
mahabharata:12:318.54	For this moon is not destroyed, though the host of gods trembling falls to earth and climbs again; the moon always wanes and is again filled.
mahabharata:12:318.55	But the sun scorches the worlds with fierce rays, taking splendour on every side, its disc ever undiminished.
mahabharata:12:318.56	Therefore I wish to go to the sun of blazing splendour; there I shall dwell, unassailable, with an inner self free of attachment.
mahabharata:12:318.57	And leaving this body in the sun's abode, I shall go with the sages to the solar splendour, very hard to bear.
mahabharata:12:318.58	I take leave of the trees, serpents, mountains, earth, directions and sky, of the gods, danavas, gandharvas, pishachas, uragas and rakshasas.
mahabharata:12:318.59	I shall enter all beings in the worlds, doubtless; let all the gods with the sages see the power of my yoga.
Then, having taken leave of the world-famous sage Narada, and having gained his permission, he went to his father.
Saluting the great-souled sage Dvaipayana, the sage Shuka circled him and took leave of Krishna.
Hearing Shuka's words, the great-souled sage, pleased, said to him again: "Ho, ho, son! Stay for today, until I satisfy my eyes with you."
Becoming indifferent, Shuka, without affection, his bonds loosed, thinking only of liberation, set his mind on going; leaving his father, the best of the twice-born went.
The great sage held himself as the scriptures prescribe, knowing the order of yoga, in order from the feet onward through the limbs.
Then, facing east, the learned one, when the sun had newly risen, composed his hands and feet and sat down humbly.
There was no flock of birds, no sound, nor any sight, where the wise son of Vyasa began to practise yoga.
He saw himself then released from his attachments; Shuka, looking at the sun, laughed a great laugh.
Taking up yoga again for the attainment of the path of liberation, he became a great lord of yogis and passed into the sky.
Then, circling the divine sage Narada, he made known his yoga to the supreme sage.
The path is seen, I have set out; blessings on you, wealth of austerity; by your grace I shall go to the desired goal, greatly radiant one.
Permitted by Narada, Dvaipayana's son saluted him, took up yoga again and entered the sky.
As far as they could and as was proper, they paid him honour, and the dwellers of heaven showered him with divine flowers.
Seeing him, all the troops of gandharvas and apsarases were astonished, and the sages and perfected ones came to supreme wonder.
Who is this sky-goer, who has attained perfection through austerity, whose body is turned downward and face upward, borne along by his eyes?
Then he of supremely steady mind, renowned in the three worlds, looking at the sun, facing east and silent, went, filling all the sky as it were with sound on every side.
Seeing him suddenly approach, all the troops of apsarases, O king, were bewildered and greatly astonished, Panchachuda and the rest, their eyes wide open.
Which deity is this, who has taken the highest path? He comes here firmly resolved, like one freed and without desire.
Then he passed the mountain named Malaya, which Urvashi and Purvachitti always frequent, and they came to the highest wonder at the Brahmarishi's son.

Ah, the concentration of understanding in a twice-born devoted to the study of the Vedas! In no long time he moves in the sky like the moon; he has gained this unsurpassed success by serving his father.
mahabharata:12:319.22	Devoted to his father, firm in austerity, a son dear to his father: how is he separated from that father, with a mind set on none other?
Hearing Urvashi's words, Shuka, knower of supreme dharma, looked toward all the directions, his mind set on her speech.
Then he looked at the sky and the earth with its mountains, woods and forests, and at the lakes and rivers.
Then all the goddesses, with joined palms, looked upon Dvaipayana's son with great respect.
Then Shuka, knower of supreme dharma, said to them: "If my father follows me, crying 'Shuka!',
then all of you together must reply; out of affection for me, you should all do this."
Hearing Shuka's words, the directions with their groves, the oceans, the rivers and the mountains replied to him on every side:
As you command, brahmana, so it shall be; when the sage speaks, we shall answer.
Leaving the eightfold tamas, he left the fivefold rajas, then the wise one left sattva; it seemed wonderful.
Then, in that eternal state, without qualities and without marks, he established himself in Brahman, like a blazing fire without smoke.
Meteors fell, the directions burned, and earthquakes appeared in that moment; it seemed wonderful.
Trees shed their branches, mountains their peaks, and with crashing sounds the Himalaya seemed to split.
The thousand-rayed sun did not shine, the fire did not blaze, lakes and rivers and oceans were shaken.
Vasava rained water, flavoured and fragrant, and the pure wind blew bearing divine scent.
He saw two incomparable divine peaks born of the Himalaya and Meru, joined, white and yellow, two lovely ones of gold and silver,
a hundred yojanas wide, across and upward, Bharata, lovely, standing toward the northern quarter.
Then, going above lovely Mandakini, with its flowering trees and groves, righteous-souled Shuka saw her.
In her troops of apsarases, delighted, played and bathed, formless, in empty shapes, and unclothed they saw Shuka.
Knowing him to be going on, his father, full of affection, took the highest path and followed behind.
But Shuka, going above the wind, making his way through the sky, showing his power, then became all beings.
Vyasa of great austerity rose and, in the twinkling of an eye, came to the place of Shuka's fall along the foremost path of great yoga.
He saw the mountain peak split in two where Shuka had gone; the sages told him his son's deed then.
Then by his father himself, with a long recitation, in a loud voice, he was cried to, "Shuka!", making the three worlds resound.
Shuka, having become all-pervading, the self of all, facing all sides, righteous-souled, replied "Bho!", making the sound resound.
Then uttering only the one-syllable cry "Bho!", the whole world, moving and unmoving, loudly echoed it back.
From then till today, sounds uttered separately in mountain caves and slopes answer for Shuka.
Having shown his power and vanished, Shuka then, abandoning the qualities of sound and the rest, reached the supreme state.
Seeing the greatness of his son of boundless splendour, he sat on the mountain slope, thinking only of his son.
Then on the bank of Mandakini the troops of apsarases playing, coming upon that sage, were all bewildered and senseless.
Some hid in the water, some went to thickets, some took up garments, seeing that best of sages.
Realising their freedom and his own attachment, the sage was pleased and also ashamed.
Surrounded by gods and gandharvas, honoured by troops of great sages, the blessed Shankara, bearing the Pinaka in hand, came to him.
Mahadeva then spoke these soothing words to Krishna Dvaipayana, tormented with grief for his son:

You chose from me of old a son equal in power to fire, earth, water, wind and space.
mahabharata:12:320.34	Such was he born, gathered by your austerity and by my power, pure, made of the splendour of Brahman.
mahabharata:12:320.35	He has attained the supreme goal, hard to reach even for gods with unmastered senses; brahmana sage, why do you grieve for him?
mahabharata:12:320.36	As long as the mountains stand and as long as the oceans stand, so long will your fame, with your son, be imperishable.
mahabharata:12:320.37	By my grace, great sage, you will always see in this world a shadow like your son, never leaving you on any side.
Consoled by the blessed Rudra himself, Bharata, the sage returned seeing the shadow, with supreme joy.
Thus, bull of the Bharatas, I have told you at length the birth and goal of Shuka, which you asked me.
The divine sage Narada told me this of old, O king, and the great yogi Vyasa too, at every step of their talks.
He who bears this holy Itihasa, joined with the dharma and purpose of liberation, intent on peace, would reach the supreme goal.
[Yudhishthira said:] Whence for him is the fixed heaven, whence the supreme highest good? By what rite should one offer to the gods and likewise to the ancestors?
And what goal would a freed one reach, and what is the nature of liberation? One gone to heaven, what should he do, so as not to fall from heaven?
Who is the god of the gods and the father of the fathers, and what is higher than that? Tell me, grandfather.
[Bhishma said:] You ask me, sinless one, a hidden question, one who knows questions; it cannot be answered by reasoning even in hundreds of years.
Except by the grace of a god, king, or by the tradition of knowledge; this account is deep and must be explained, slayer of foes.
On this they recount this ancient Itihasa, the conversation of Narada and the sage Narayana.
For Narayana, the self of all, the eternal, fourfold in form, was born as Dharma's son; so my father told me.
In the Krita age, great king, long ago in the Svayambhuva interval, Nara and Narayana, and Hari and Krishna.
That vehicle has eight wheels, charming, joined with beings; there those two first lords of the world, lean, with veins showing,
hard to behold even for the gods by austerity and splendour; he whom they favour deserves to see the two gods.
Surely, urged by the heart's desire with their consent, Narada fell from the peak of the great mountain Meru onto Gandhamadana.
A very great being, he roamed all the worlds; swift, he came, O king, to that place, the hermitage at Badari.
At the time of their daily rites curiosity arose in him: "This is the whole abode in which the worlds are established.
Always asuras, gandharvas, sages and kinnaras, lickers of the tongue... this one form was born first and then fourfold.
The great line of Dharma's family has been increased by these. Ah, today Dharma is favoured here by these gods, by Nara and Narayana, and by Krishna Hari.
There Krishna and Hari, for some other reason, stand foremost in dharma and established in austerity.
These two are the supreme abode; what is their daily rite? They are fathers of all beings and glorious deities; which deity do they worship, or which ancestors, these two of great mind?"
Thus reflecting in his mind with devotion to Narayana, he suddenly appeared near the two gods.
When the offerings to gods and ancestors had been made, he was looked upon by them and duly honoured as the scripture prescribes.
Seeing that great, unprecedented marvel of extended rites, the blessed sage Narada sat down, greatly pleased.
Looking at Narayana with a calm inner self, he bowed to Mahadeva and spoke these words:

You are sung in the Vedas with the Puranas, with their limbs and subsidiary limbs, unborn, eternal, the creator, held to be the unsurpassed nectar; in you, all this world, past and future, is established.
mahabharata:12:321.25	All four stages of life, god, rooted in the householder's life, worship you day after day, standing in many forms.
mahabharata:12:321.26	You are father and mother of all the world, its eternal teacher; whom, then, do you worship today as god, whom as father? We do not know.
[The Blessed One said:] This should not be spoken, yet it is to be told, the eternal secret of the self; to you, Brahmana, being devoted, I shall tell it as it is.
That which is subtle, unknowable, unmanifest, unmoving, fixed, free of senses, of objects of the senses and of all beings,

that is the inner self of beings, called the knower of the field; beyond the three qualities, it is conceived as the person; from it the unmanifest was born, threefold in quality, best of the twice-born.

The unmanifest standing in manifest being, that imperishable nature, know that as the womb of us two, which is both being and non-being; for it is worshipped by us two in the rites for gods and ancestors.
There is no other beyond it, father, god or twice-born; it is to be known as the self of us two; therefore we worship it.
By it, Brahmana, this limit that supports the world was laid down: that the rites for gods and ancestors are to be done; such is its command.
Brahma, Sthanu, Manu, Daksha, Bhrigu, Dharma, Tapas, Dama, Marichi, Angiras, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Vasishtha, Parameshthi, Vivasvan and Soma, and Kardama as well, and Krodha and Vikrita, who are named,
twenty-one arose, who are remembered as the Prajapatis; they worship the eternal limit of that god.
Knowing in truth the rites for gods and ancestors as his, the best of the twice-born also know what has come to them by themselves.
Whatever embodied beings even in heaven bow to him, by his grace go to the goal whose fruit he has ordained.
Those who are free of the seventeen qualities and of action, having given up the fifteen parts, are certainly liberated.
The goal of the freed, Brahmana, is conceived as the knower of the field; he is said to be all-pervading and without qualities.
He is seen by the yoga of knowledge, and we two came forth from him; thus knowing, we worship that eternal self.
The Vedas and the stages of life, standing in many bodies, worship that primal one with devotion, and he gives them their goal.
But those in the world who are formed by him and stand in single-minded devotion have this in addition: that they enter him.
Thus this hidden teaching has been told to you, Narada, with devotion and love, brahmana sage, and heard by you with devotion to us.
[Narada said:] "For the sake of which, self-born, this excellent birth in four forms in the house of Dharma, let that be accomplished today for the good of the world; I go to see your primal nature.
The Vedas are well studied by me, lord of the world; austerity has been practised; no untruth has been spoken before; I constantly honour the teachers, and I have never divulged another's secret.

The four are guarded by me as the tradition says; I am always equal to enemy and friend; having taken refuge in that primal god constantly, I choose him with single-minded devotion ceaselessly; with these distinctions, of pure sattva, why should I not see the infinite lord?"
Hearing those words of Parameshthi's son, Narayana, protector of the Satvata dharma, said to Narada, "Go," having honoured him by the rites of his own order.
Dismissed, Parameshthi's son honoured that ancient sage and sprang into the sky with the highest speed; then he suddenly vanished on Meru.
There the sage stayed for a moment, and reaching a solitary peak of the mountain, looking to the north-west, he saw something of wonderful form.
North of the Milk Ocean is a great island named Shveta, said by the learned to be thirty-two thousand yojanas above Meru.
There the men are beyond the senses, without food, motionless, very fragrant, white, free of all sin, with eyes that blind the men who do evil.
With sixty teeth, white, with eight tusks, with tongues they lick the sun-like face on every side.
With devotion to the god from whom the universe arose, from whom all worlds are born, the Vedas, dharmas, sages and calm gods are all his emanations.
[Yudhishthira said:] Those men, beyond the senses, without food, motionless, fragrant: how were they born, and what is their highest goal?
The mark of men who are freed here, best of Bharatas, is this, that they dwell in Shvetadvipa.
Therefore cut my doubt; great is my curiosity; you are the delight of all stories, and we have come to you.
[Bhishma said:] This story, king, is long, and I heard it in my father's presence; it must be told to you, for it is remembered as the essence.
There was a lord of the earth named Uparichara, famed as Indra's friend, devoted to Narayana Hari.
Righteous, always devoted, unwearied toward the ancestors, he gained empire of old by Narayana's boon.
Following the Satvata rite, which first issued from the sun's mouth, he worshipped the lord of the gods, and with the remainder the ancestors.
With the ancestors' remainder he shared with brahmanas and dependants, eating the remains, intent on truth, harming no beings; devoted with all his being to Janardana, god of gods.
To him bearing devotion to Narayana, scourge of foes, Shakra himself gave a shared couch and seat, god-like king.
Self, kingdom, wealth, wife and vehicles: all this belongs to the blessed one: so he always regarded it.
Voluntary, occasional and constant sacrificial rites, all the highest acts, he performed with composure, following the Satvata rule.
In that great soul's house the foremost knowers of the Pancharatra ate first, the refuge told by the Blessed One.
As he ruled the kingdom by dharma, slaying enemies, no untrue speech occurred, his mind was not corrupted, and he did not do the slightest sin with his body.
Those famed sages, the seven Chitrashikhandins, becoming of one mind, composed the supreme scripture that was told.
Marichi, Atri, Angiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu and the greatly radiant Vasishtha: these are the Chitrashikhandins.
These are the seven natures, and the Svayambhuva is the eighth; by these the world is supported, and from them the scripture issued.
One-pointed, self-controlled, sages intent on restraint, thinking of the worlds: "This is the good, this is Brahman, this is the unsurpassed benefit," then composed the scripture.
There dharma, wealth and desire, and liberation afterwards, are told, and various limits established in heaven and on earth.
Having worshipped by austerity the god Hari Narayana, the lord, for a divine thousand years, all of them with the sages,
then, instructed by Narayana, the goddess Sarasvati entered all those sages, wishing the good of the worlds.
Then it was rightly set going by ascetic twice-born in word, meaning and reason; this was born of the first creation.
That scripture, adorned from the beginning with the sound of Om, was formed by the sages where that merciful one was.
Then the blessed one, pleased, unseen, in a body not shown, the Supreme Person, spoke to all those sages:

This excellent work of a hundred thousand verses has been made, by which dharma proceeds for the whole system of the world.

Dhanushaksha, Raibhya, Arvavasu, Paravasu the sage, Medhatithi, and the great sage Tandya,

in the northern part of Meru, near the Milk Ocean, at the place where we practised most severe austerity: 'How might we see the god Narayana?'
